title: Floating & Sinking
strapline: Will it float or will it sink? Drop it in, watch, and find out you were sometimes wrong.
intent: Testing what floats and what sinks is real scientific enquiry — children predict, test, observe and are sometimes surprised, which is exactly where thinking sharpens.
Sorting objects into 'floaters' and 'sinkers' is genuine classification, and the surprises push children to look harder at why.
Handling a wide range of objects in water builds vocabulary — heavy, light, hollow, solid, metal, wooden — tied to what they can see happen.
Trying to make a sinker float, or load a floating boat until it sinks, invites persistent problem-solving and early ideas about weight and shape.
The activity is calm, absorbing and endlessly repeatable, and children can lead their own investigations at their own pace.
implementation: Offer a deep tub and a rich mix of objects — cork, stone, metal spoon, plastic lid, sponge, coin, apple — and two hoops or trays to sort into.
Always ask for a prediction first: 'float or sink? why do you think so?' — then drop it in and compare.
Welcome the surprises out loud: 'you thought it would sink — but look! What's different about this one?'
Set challenges that deepen the thinking: 'can you make this heavy thing float?', 'how many pebbles before the boat goes under?'
Model precise words as objects go in — hollow, solid, heavy for its size — and let children start to use them.
Keep it child-led; the value is in their own testing, sorting and wondering, not in reaching a 'right answer'.
key_questions: Float or sink? Why do you think so?
You thought it would sink — but look! What's different about this one?
Can you make this heavy thing float?
How many pebbles before the boat goes under?
What do all the floaters have in common?

Children take on persistent problem-solving — making a sinker float, loading a boat until it sinks.
Children lead their own calm, repeatable investigations at their own pace.
